title: Copying: the rule of three, five and zero

notes: Loadout owns no raw pointers, so the compiler's copy is already a deep copy.
Changing b doesn't touch a: each has its own string and vector.
std::move(b) lets c take b's insides; b is left valid but empty (its size is 0 here).
No destructor, copy or move code was written: that's the rule of zero.

exercises.title: Deep copy a waypoint path
exercises.prompt: Path owns a heap array of waypoints. Finish its copy constructor and copy assignment so that copies are deep: a copy has the same size and values, but its own array, so changing one never changes the other. Copy assignment must work between paths of different sizes and must be safe for self-assignment (p = p).

tests.call: []{ Path a(3); a.set(0, 7); a.set(2, 9); Path b(a); return b.get(0) * 10 + b.get(2); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: The copy constructor must copy each value from other.points.

tests.call: []{ Path a(2); a.set(0, 1); Path b(a); b.set(0, 5); return a.get(0) * 10 + b.get(0); }()
[]{ Path a(3); a.set(2, 4); Path b(1); b = a; a.set(2, 8); return b.size() * 10 + b.get(2); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Assignment needs a new array of other's size, then the values, then delete[] the old array.

tests.call: []{ Path a(2); a.set(1, 6); Path& r = a; a = r; return a.get(1); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: p = p: don't delete the array you're about to copy from.

tests.call: []{ Path a(2); a.set(0, 3); Path b(5); b = a; Path c(1); c = b; c.set(0, 0); return std::to_string(b.size()) + std::to_string(b.get(0)) + std::to_string(c.size()); }()

hints: Copy constructor: for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) points[i] = other.points[i];
Assignment: if (this == &other) return *this; then build a fresh array, copy into it, delete[] points, and set points and count.
Building the new array before deleting the old one also makes it safe if new throws.

exercises.title: A move-only audio channel

tests.call: []{ int before = Channel::open; { Channel a(3); Channel b(std::move(a)); if (a.owns() || b.getId() != 3) return -99; if (Channel::open - before != 1) return -50; } return Channel::open - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: After the move, a must own nothing (id -1) so only b closes the channel.

tests.call: []{ int before = Channel::open; { Channel a(1); Channel b(2); b = std::move(a); if (b.getId() != 1 || a.owns()) return -99; if (Channel::open - before != 1) return -50; } return Channel::open - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: b already owned channel 2: close it (open--) before taking channel 1.

tests.call: []{ int before = Channel::open; { std::vector<Channel> v; v.emplace_back(1); v.emplace_back(2); v.emplace_back(3); if (Channel::open - before != 3) return -1; } return Channel::open - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: When the vector grows it moves channels; the move constructor must leave the old one empty.

tests.why: Mark the move operations noexcept so std::vector will use them.

hints: Channel(const Channel&) = delete; Channel& operator=(const Channel&) = delete;
Move assignment: if (this != &other) { if (id >= 0) open--; id = other.id; other.id = -1; } return *this;

exercises.title: Rule of zero scoreboard
exercises.prompt: This Scoreboard owns a raw array and crashes when copied. Rewrite it with the rule of zero: keep the same public functions (explicit Scoreboard(std::string title), void add(int score), int count() const, int best() const (0 when empty), std::string getTitle() const), but store the scores in a std::vector<int>, and write no destructor, no copy functions and no new or delete. Copies must be independent.

tests.call: []{ Scoreboard s("Wave 1"); s.add(40); s.add(90); s.add(65); return s.best() * 10 + s.count(); }()
[]{ Scoreboard a("Wave 1"); a.add(10); Scoreboard b = a; b.add(99); return a.best() * 1000 + b.best(); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: With a std::vector member, the compiler's copy is already deep.

tests.call: []{ Scoreboard a("A"); a.add(5); Scoreboard b("B"); b = a; return b.getTitle() + std::to_string(b.count()); }()
[]{ Scoreboard s("Big"); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) s.add(i); return s.best() * 1000 + s.count(); }()
[]{ Scoreboard s("Neg"); s.add(-5); s.add(-2); return s.best(); }()

tests.why: Rule of zero: no delete (and no = delete either) is needed.
Use a std::vector<int> instead of new.

hints: Replace int* scores, n and cap with std::vector<int> scores; (add #include <vector>).
add becomes scores.push_back(score); count is scores.size().
Delete the destructor entirely: the vector frees itself.

quiz.q: A class has a raw pointer member and the default copy. Path b = a; What does b get?
choices: Its own copy of the array
The same address: a shallow copy
quiz.why: Members are copied one by one; a pointer copies as an address.

quiz.q: The rule of three says that if you write a destructor, you probably also need...
choices: a copy constructor and copy assignment
quiz.why: All three manage the same owned resource.

quiz.q: Why check this == &other in copy assignment?
choices: So a = a doesn't delete the data before copying it
quiz.why: Self-assignment would free the array you're about to copy from.

quiz.q: What does Channel(const Channel&) = delete; do?
choices: Makes any attempt to copy a Channel a compile error
quiz.why: = delete removes that function; the compiler refuses copies.

quiz.q: A class whose members are std::string, std::vector and std::unique_ptr needs which special functions?
quiz.why: The members manage themselves; the class is automatically correct (and move-only because of unique_ptr).

cards.a: Shallow copies the pointer; deep copies what it points at.
Destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment: need one, need all three.
Move constructor and move assignment (mark them noexcept).
Use members that manage themselves (vector, string, smart pointers) and write none of them.

explain: Explain the difference between a shallow and a deep copy, and why the rule of zero avoids the problem altogether.
